questions.title: Which of the following changes increases the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
questions.question: Which of the following changes increases the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?

options.A: A decrease in plasma (glomerular capillary) oncotic pressure
options.B: An increase in Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure
options.D: An increase in plasma oncotic pressure

explanations.A: Correct. GFR is driven by the net filtration pressure across the glomerular capillary, which equals the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure minus the glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (the main opposing force to filtration). Lowering plasma oncotic pressure — as happens with hypoalbuminemia — reduces this opposing force, so more of the hydrostatic pressure is available to drive fluid out of the capillary, increasing GFR.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration, so an increase in it (e.g. from obstruction) would decrease, not increase, GFR.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Afferent arteriolar constriction reduces glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and renal plasma flow, decreasing GFR.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased plasma oncotic pressure increases the opposing force to filtration, decreasing GFR — the opposite direction from what the question asks.

questions.title: Which of the following is used to measure the maximal secretory capacity (secretory power) of the kidney?
questions.question: Which of the following is used to measure the maximal secretory capacity (secretory power) of the kidney?

explanations.A: Correct. PAH is both filtered and, once plasma PAH concentration is raised high enough to saturate the proximal tubular organic anion transporters, actively secreted into the tubule at its maximal rate. The transport maximum for PAH (Tm PAH) therefore measures the kidney's maximal tubular secretory capacity, just as Tm glucose measures maximal tubular reabsorptive capacity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, which is what makes its clearance a measure of GFR, not of tubular secretory capacity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatinine clearance approximates GFR (with a small secretory component that makes it a slight overestimate), not a measure of maximal secretory power.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tm glucose measures the maximal rate of tubular reabsorption, the opposite direction of transport from secretion.

questions.title: Bartter syndrome is characteristically associated with which of the following electrolyte abnormalities?
questions.question: Bartter syndrome is characteristically associated with which of the following electrolyte abnormalities?

explanations.A: Correct. Bartter syndrome is an inherited tubulopathy caused by defective salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, functionally mimicking chronic loop diuretic use. This produces volume depletion that activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and the resulting hyperaldosteronism drives renal potassium wasting, so patients characteristically present with hypokalemia together with metabolic alkalosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bartter syndrome causes potassium wasting (via secondary hyperaldosteronism), producing hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bartter syndrome causes salt wasting with generally normal-to-low blood pressure, not hypernatremia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bartter syndrome is associated with hypercalciuria (urinary calcium loss) but typically normal or low, not high, serum calcium.

questions.title: According to the principle of glomerulotubular balance, what happens to peritubular capillary oncotic pressure when GFR increases (at constant renal plasma flow)?
questions.question: According to the principle of glomerulotubular balance, what happens to peritubular capillary oncotic pressure when GFR increases (at constant renal plasma flow)?

options.C: Peritubular capillary oncotic pressure is unaffected by GFR
options.D: Peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure increases while oncotic pressure falls

explanations.A: Correct. When GFR rises relative to renal plasma flow, the filtration fraction (GFR/RPF) increases, meaning a larger share of plasma water leaves the glomerular capillaries as filtrate while plasma proteins stay behind in the blood that continues on to the peritubular capillaries. This concentrates protein in the post-glomerular blood, raising peritubular capillary oncotic pressure, which in turn enhances proximal tubular fluid reabsorption — the physiological basis of glomerulotubular balance, which keeps the fraction of filtered load reabsorbed roughly constant despite changes in GFR.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peritubular capillary oncotic pressure rises, not falls, when filtration fraction increases, since protein is left more concentrated in the blood that did not filter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peritubular capillary oncotic pressure is directly linked to filtration fraction and therefore does change with GFR at a given renal plasma flow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure is set mainly by efferent arteriolar resistance, not directly driven up by GFR in this way, and it is the rise (not a fall) in oncotic pressure that mediates glomerulotubular balance.

questions.title: Which of the following removes water from the renal medullary interstitium as part of the countercurrent exchange mechanism?
questions.question: Which of the following removes water from the renal medullary interstitium as part of the countercurrent exchange mechanism?

options.A: The ascending limb of the vasa recta
options.B: The descending limb of the vasa recta
options.C: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
options.D: The descending limb of the loop of Henle

explanations.A: Correct. The vasa recta act as passive countercurrent exchangers that preserve, rather than dissipate, the medullary osmotic gradient. As blood ascends back toward the cortex in the ascending limb of the vasa recta, it re-enters progressively less hyperosmotic interstitium, so water that had entered the descending limb (and solute that diffused in along the way) moves back out of the vessel into the blood, effectively removing the excess water that entered the medulla and carrying it away.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The descending limb of the vasa recta is where water leaves the blood and solute enters as the blood descends into the increasingly hyperosmotic medulla, the opposite direction of net water movement from what the question asks.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water; it actively transports NaCl out of the tubule to establish the medullary gradient but does not itself remove interstitial water via blood flow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The descending limb of the loop of Henle is where tubular fluid loses water into the hyperosmotic interstitium, adding water to it rather than removing it.

questions.title: Ammonia (NH3/NH4+) is an especially effective urinary buffer in which of the following locations?
questions.question: Ammonia (NH3/NH4+) is an especially effective urinary buffer in which of the following locations?

explanations.A: Correct. The renal tubular epithelium (chiefly the proximal tubule) synthesizes ammonia from glutamine and secretes it into the tubular lumen, where it combines with secreted H+ to form ammonium (NH4+), which is then trapped in the lumen (since the epithelium is far less permeable to the charged NH4+ than to neutral NH3) and excreted in the urine. Because the kidney can increase ammonia synthesis and secretion on demand — unlike the fixed buffering capacity of phosphate — the ammonia buffer system gives the kidney a large, adaptable capacity to excrete the daily acid load and regenerate bicarbonate, making it especially effective specifically in this organ.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lungs regulate acid-base balance by adjusting CO2 (respiratory) excretion, not by generating and excreting an ammonia buffer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ammonia buffering is a renal tubular secretory process, not simply a plasma buffer reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While gut bacteria produce ammonia, it is the kidney's regulated synthesis and urinary trapping of ammonia that makes it a titratable, adaptable acid-base buffer system.

questions.title: Which of the following conditions is associated with a decrease in urinary titratable acid excretion?
questions.question: Which of the following conditions is associated with a decrease in urinary titratable acid excretion?

options.B: Chronic kidney disease with metabolic acidosis

explanations.A: Correct. Titratable acid excretion depends on renal H+ secretion, which is stimulated by systemic acidosis and suppressed by alkalosis. Psychogenic hyperventilation blows off CO2 and produces a respiratory alkalosis, which reduces the tubular drive to secrete H+ and therefore decreases urinary titratable acid excretion, the opposite of what occurs in an acidotic state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chronic kidney disease with metabolic acidosis reflects reduced net acid excretion capacity overall, but the acidemic stimulus that is present still tends to drive what H+ secretory capacity remains, unlike the alkalosis of hyperventilation which actively suppresses it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a severe acidemic state that maximally stimulates renal H+ secretion and titratable acid excretion (along with ammoniagenesis), not a state that decreases it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic respiratory acidosis (CO2 retention) stimulates, rather than decreases, renal H+ secretion and titratable acid excretion as a compensatory response.

questions.title: Which of the following acid-base disturbances is characteristically found in chronic kidney disease?
questions.question: Which of the following acid-base disturbances is characteristically found in chronic kidney disease?

explanations.A: Correct. As nephron mass and function decline in chronic kidney disease, the kidneys' capacity to excrete the daily fixed acid load (via ammoniagenesis and titratable acid excretion) and to regenerate bicarbonate progressively falls short of dietary acid production, leading to a chronic, typically normal-anion-gap (early) transitioning to increased-anion-gap (advanced) metabolic acidosis. This retained-acid, reduced-excretion state is one of the classic systemic complications of chronic kidney disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Metabolic alkalosis is not a characteristic feature of CKD; it more typically arises from causes such as vomiting, diuretic use, or mineralocorticoid excess.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Respiratory acidosis arises from impaired ventilation (a pulmonary/respiratory problem), not from failing renal acid excretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis arises from hyperventilation, unrelated to the renal acid-excretion defect of CKD.

questions.title: Which of the following is a recognized cause of hyperkalemia through cellular potassium release?
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized cause of hyperkalemia through cellular potassium release?

explanations.A: Correct. Crush injury causes rhabdomyolysis, in which damaged skeletal muscle cells release their large intracellular potassium stores directly into the extracellular fluid, producing a rapid rise in serum potassium that can be severe and life-threatening, especially once reperfusion of the injured tissue occurs. This is a classic cause of hyperkalemia through cell lysis/release rather than through impaired renal excretion alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Insulin drives potassium into cells (via stimulating the Na+/K+-ATPase), lowering, not raising, serum potassium — it is used therapeutically to treat hyperkalemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Beta-2 agonists also drive potassium into cells and lower serum potassium, and are likewise used as an emergency treatment for hyperkalemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alkalosis promotes potassium shift into cells (in exchange for H+ leaving cells to buffer the alkalosis), tending to lower, not raise, serum potassium; acidosis is the acid-base disturbance associated with hyperkalemia.

questions.title: Which of the following characterizes potassium and hydrogen ion handling in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct?
questions.question: Which of the following characterizes potassium and hydrogen ion handling in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct?

options.A: Potassium and hydrogen ion secretion by intercalated/principal cells compete with each other
options.B: Potassium and hydrogen ions are always secreted in direct proportion to one another
options.C: Potassium secretion is entirely independent of acid-base status
options.D: Hydrogen ion secretion occurs exclusively in the proximal tubule, not the distal nephron

explanations.A: Correct. In the distal tubule and collecting duct, principal cells secrete K+ while intercalated cells secrete H+, and these two secretory processes compete with (reciprocally influence) each other because both are linked to the same driving forces (electrochemical gradients set up by Na+ reabsorption) and to intracellular pH/potassium handling. This is why, for example, acidosis (which favors H+ secretion) tends to reduce K+ secretion and predispose to hyperkalemia, while alkalosis favors K+ secretion and can produce hypokalemia — a reciprocal, competitive relationship rather than a fixed proportional one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The relationship is reciprocal/competitive, not a fixed direct proportion — favoring one ion's secretion tends to come at the expense of the other's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Potassium secretion is very much influenced by acid-base status, which is precisely the basis of the H-K competition described here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While the proximal tubule reabsorbs the bulk of filtered bicarbonate via H+ secretion, the distal nephron (intercalated cells) also secretes H+ and is critical for final urinary acidification.

questions.learning_objective: Potassium and hydrogen ion secretion in the distal tubule and collecting duct compete with each other

questions.title: Which of the following would be expected to decrease glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
questions.question: Which of the following would be expected to decrease glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?

options.A: A ureteric (renal) stone causing urinary tract obstruction
options.C: A decrease in plasma oncotic pressure

explanations.A: Correct. Obstruction from a renal or ureteric stone raises the hydrostatic pressure within Bowman's capsule and the tubule upstream of the obstruction. Since Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure directly opposes glomerular filtration, this back-pressure lowers net filtration pressure and reduces GFR, and if prolonged, obstruction also triggers vasoconstrictive and structural changes that further impair filtration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Afferent arteriolar dilatation increases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and renal plasma flow, increasing (not decreasing) GFR.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A decrease in plasma oncotic pressure reduces the main force opposing filtration, increasing GFR.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mild efferent arteriolar constriction raises glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and, up to a point, increases GFR (this is the basis of RAAS-mediated GFR preservation in low-flow states); it is only severe efferent constriction that eventually drops renal plasma flow enough to reduce GFR.

questions.title: A man lost in the desert becomes progressively dehydrated. Which of the following is the primary physiological trigger for his subsequent thirst and ADH release?
questions.question: A man lost in the desert becomes progressively dehydrated. Which of the following is the primary physiological trigger for his subsequent thirst and ADH release?

options.A: Stimulation of hypothalamic osmoreceptors by rising plasma osmolarity
options.B: Stimulation of carotid body chemoreceptors by hypoxia
options.C: Suppression of atrial natriuretic peptide release
options.D: Direct stimulation of the posterior pituitary by falling blood pressure alone

explanations.A: Correct. As the man loses free water through sweating and insensible losses without adequate intake, his plasma osmolarity rises above the normal set point. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors are exquisitely sensitive to small changes in effective osmolarity, and they detect this rise and respond by triggering both the sensation of thirst and increased ADH (vasopressin) release from the posterior pituitary. This ADH release promotes water reabsorption in the collecting duct, conserving water and diluting the plasma back toward normal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carotid body chemoreceptors respond mainly to arterial PO2/PCO2/pH, not to plasma osmolarity, and are not the primary driver of thirst and ADH release in simple dehydration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Atrial natriuretic peptide is released in response to atrial stretch (volume expansion) and is suppressed, not the primary trigger, in a volume-depleted, hyperosmolar dehydration state.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While large falls in blood volume/pressure can also stimulate ADH release via baroreceptors, the earlier and more sensitive trigger in straightforward dehydration is the osmoreceptor response to rising plasma osmolarity, not blood pressure acting directly on the pituitary.

questions.learning_objective: Rising plasma osmolarity from dehydration stimulates hypothalamic osmoreceptors to trigger thirst and ADH release

questions.title: Which of the following best describes normal renal blood flow?
questions.question: Which of the following best describes normal renal blood flow?

options.A: It represents approximately 20-25% of cardiac output
options.B: It represents approximately 5% of cardiac output
options.C: It represents approximately 50% of cardiac output
options.D: It is distributed evenly between the renal cortex and medulla

explanations.A: Correct. Despite the kidneys making up only a small fraction of total body mass, they receive a disproportionately large share of cardiac output, roughly 20-25%. This reflects their high metabolic demand for filtration and the large blood volume that must be processed to filter plasma and regulate the body's fluid and electrolyte balance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 5% substantially underestimates renal blood flow; the kidneys receive a much larger fraction of cardiac output than this.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 50% overestimates renal blood flow; that level of flow is not physiologically accurate for the kidneys at rest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renal blood flow is markedly uneven — the cortex receives the great majority of flow (needed for filtration), while the medulla receives only a small fraction, which helps preserve the medullary concentration gradient.

questions.title: Combining an anti-mineralocorticoid (e.g. spironolactone) with an ACE inhibitor carries a particular risk of which of the following?
questions.question: Combining an anti-mineralocorticoid (e.g. spironolactone) with an ACE inhibitor carries a particular risk of which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II formation and therefore aldosterone secretion, while anti-mineralocorticoids (aldosterone receptor antagonists) directly block aldosterone's action at the principal cell; both mechanisms independently reduce distal nephron potassium secretion. Combining the two drug classes produces an additive, clinically significant risk of hyperkalemia, which is why potassium must be monitored closely when they are co-prescribed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both drug classes reduce, rather than promote, urinary potassium loss, so the combination raises (not lowers) serum potassium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both drug classes tend to promote natriuresis (sodium loss) rather than sodium retention, so hypernatremia is not the characteristic risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. By reducing aldosterone-driven H+ secretion as well as K+ secretion, this combination if anything favors a mild acidosis (hyperkalemic distal renal tubular acidosis-like picture) rather than alkalosis.

questions.learning_objective: Combining an ACE inhibitor with an anti-mineralocorticoid carries an additive risk of hyperkalemia

questions.title: Which of the following is a recognized endocrine function of the kidney?
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized endocrine function of the kidney?

explanations.A: Correct. In addition to its filtration and excretory roles, the kidney is an endocrine organ: peritubular fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex and outer medulla sense tissue hypoxia and secrete erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. The kidney also activates vitamin D and secretes renin, but among the options given, erythropoietin secretion is the correct recognized renal endocrine function.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Insulin is secreted by pancreatic beta cells, not the kidney.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thyroid-stimulating hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary, not the kidney.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Parathyroid hormone is secreted by the parathyroid glands; the kidney is a target organ for PTH action and activates vitamin D, but it does not secrete PTH itself.

questions.title: Among freely filtered substances, which of the following has the lowest renal clearance under normal physiological conditions?
questions.question: Among freely filtered substances, which of the following has the lowest renal clearance under normal physiological conditions?

explanations.A: Correct. Glucose is freely filtered at the glomerulus but, under normal conditions (plasma glucose below the renal threshold), is almost completely reabsorbed by sodium-glucose cotransporters in the proximal tubule, so essentially none of the filtered glucose appears in the final urine. Because clearance reflects the volume of plasma cleared of a substance per unit time, and normal urinary glucose excretion is near zero, glucose has an essentially zero (the lowest) renal clearance among substances that are filtered, unlike inulin (cleared at the GFR) or PAH (cleared at a very high rate reflecting near-complete secretion in addition to filtration).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inulin is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR — a moderate, not the lowest, clearance value.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatinine is filtered and also modestly secreted, giving it a clearance slightly higher than GFR, well above glucose's near-zero clearance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PAH is both filtered and almost completely secreted (at low plasma concentrations), giving it the highest clearance of these options, approximating renal plasma flow — the opposite extreme from glucose.

questions.title: Complete reabsorption of filtered glucose in the proximal tubule occurs under which of the following conditions?
questions.question: Complete reabsorption of filtered glucose in the proximal tubule occurs under which of the following conditions?

options.A: When the filtered glucose load is below the renal (tubular) threshold
options.B: Only when plasma glucose exceeds the transport maximum (Tm) for glucose
options.D: Regardless of the filtered glucose load, glucose is never fully reabsorbed

explanations.A: Correct. As long as the filtered load of glucose (plasma glucose concentration times GFR) stays below the renal threshold — the point at which the reabsorptive sodium-glucose cotransporters in the proximal tubule become saturated — essentially all filtered glucose is reabsorbed and none appears in the urine. Once the filtered load exceeds this threshold (transporters saturated, at or beyond Tm glucose), reabsorption can no longer keep pace and glucose begins to spill into the urine (glucosuria).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exceeding Tm glucose is precisely when reabsorption becomes incomplete and glucosuria occurs — the opposite of the complete-reabsorption condition described in the question.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperglycemia, if it pushes the filtered load above the renal threshold, is what causes glucose to appear in the urine, not what ensures complete reabsorption.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Under normal physiological plasma glucose concentrations, filtered glucose load stays below threshold and is essentially completely reabsorbed; the statement that it is never fully reabsorbed is incorrect.

questions.learning_objective: Filtered glucose is completely reabsorbed as long as the filtered load stays below the renal threshold

questions.title: Renal autoregulation of blood flow and GFR is characterized by which of the following?
questions.question: Renal autoregulation of blood flow and GFR is characterized by which of the following?

options.A: It is largely myogenic in origin, with a contribution from tubuloglomerular feedback
options.B: It depends entirely on sympathetic nervous system activity
options.C: It is mediated primarily by circulating angiotensin II acting on the efferent arteriole
options.D: It fails to maintain renal blood flow or GFR over any range of arterial pressure

explanations.A: Correct. Renal autoregulation keeps renal blood flow and GFR relatively constant across a wide range of arterial pressures (roughly 80-180 mmHg) through two intrinsic mechanisms: the myogenic response, in which afferent arteriolar smooth muscle constricts in response to stretch from increased pressure, and tubuloglomerular feedback, in which increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa (from a higher GFR) triggers afferent arteriolar constriction. Because these mechanisms are intrinsic to the kidney itself, autoregulation persists even in a denervated or isolated, perfused kidney.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Autoregulation is intrinsic to the kidney and persists even without sympathetic innervation (as in a denervated kidney), so it does not depend entirely on the sympathetic nervous system.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While angiotensin II does preferentially constrict the efferent arteriole and helps preserve GFR in low-flow states, it is not the primary mediator of the myogenic/tubuloglomerular feedback autoregulatory response.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Autoregulation is specifically defined by its ability to maintain relatively constant renal blood flow and GFR across a defined pressure range, not by a failure to do so.

questions.title: Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in the proximal convoluted tubule requires the activity of which of the following?
questions.question: Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in the proximal convoluted tubule requires the activity of which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption depends on carbonic anhydrase acting at two sites: within the tubular lumen (brush border isoform), it catalyzes the dehydration of secreted-H+-derived carbonic acid into CO2 and water so CO2 can diffuse into the cell, and within the cytoplasm, it catalyzes the reverse reaction, regenerating carbonic acid that dissociates into H+ (resecreted into the lumen) and bicarbonate (reabsorbed across the basolateral membrane into blood). Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g. acetazolamide) block this process and produce a bicarbonaturic diuresis, which is direct pharmacological evidence for the enzyme's essential role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone acts mainly on the distal nephron to promote Na+ reabsorption and K+/H+ secretion, not on proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption via carbonic anhydrase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ADH regulates collecting duct water permeability and is not required for proximal bicarbonate reabsorption.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Parathyroid hormone acts on calcium and phosphate handling in the kidney, not on the carbonic-anhydrase-dependent bicarbonate reabsorption mechanism.

questions.title: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin primarily in response to which of the following?
questions.question: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin primarily in response to which of the following?

options.A: A drop in afferent arteriolar perfusion pressure
options.B: A rise in afferent arteriolar perfusion pressure
options.C: An increase in NaCl delivery to the macula densa

explanations.A: Correct. Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriolar wall act as intrarenal baroreceptors, sensing a fall in perfusion pressure (as occurs with volume depletion, hemorrhage, or renal artery stenosis) as reduced stretch of the arteriolar wall; this reduced stretch is a direct stimulus for renin release. Renin then initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade, ultimately promoting sodium and water retention and vasoconstriction to help restore blood pressure and perfusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A rise in perfusion pressure increases arteriolar wall stretch, which suppresses, rather than stimulates, renin release.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renin release is instead stimulated by decreased (not increased) NaCl delivery to the macula densa, which signals reduced GFR/perfusion via tubuloglomerular feedback.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is sympathetic (beta-1 adrenergic), not parasympathetic, stimulation that promotes renin release from juxtaglomerular cells.

questions.title: Which segment of the nephron shows essentially no net reabsorption of sodium?
questions.question: Which segment of the nephron shows essentially no net reabsorption of sodium?

options.A: The descending thin limb of the loop of Henle
options.C: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

explanations.A: Correct. The descending thin limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to water but has very low permeability to sodium and other solutes, and it lacks the active sodium-transport machinery (such as the Na-K-ATPase-driven NKCC2 or NCC transporters) found elsewhere in the nephron. Water leaves this segment passively as it descends into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, but sodium is essentially left behind in the tubular fluid, so there is no meaningful net sodium reabsorption here. This property is exactly what makes the descending limb a passive, water-permeable limb of the countercurrent multiplier, in contrast to the water-impermeable, sodium-transporting ascending limb.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs roughly two-thirds of filtered sodium, driven by the basolateral Na-K-ATPase and multiple apical cotransporters and exchangers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs sodium (with chloride and potassium) via the apical NKCC2 cotransporter, and is impermeable to water — the opposite pairing from the descending limb.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The distal convoluted tubule actively reabsorbs sodium chloride via the thiazide-sensitive NCC cotransporter.

questions.title: Which of the following increases the effectiveness of a chemical buffer system?
questions.question: Which of the following increases the effectiveness of a chemical buffer system?

options.A: A high concentration of the buffer pair
options.B: A buffer pKa far removed from the surrounding fluid's pH
options.C: Rapid excretion of the buffer from the body
options.D: A markedly unequal ratio of the buffer's base to acid forms

explanations.A: Correct. A buffer's capacity to resist a change in pH depends directly on how much of the buffer pair is present: the more buffer molecules available, the more added acid or base can be absorbed before the buffer pair is used up and the pH begins to swing. This is why body fluids with abundant buffer (such as bicarbonate in plasma or phosphate and ammonia in the renal tubule) can accommodate large acid loads with only small pH changes. Buffering effectiveness is therefore a function of both concentration and how close the pKa is to the operating pH, but concentration alone is sufficient to increase effectiveness even when pKa is fixed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A buffer works best when its pKa is close to the surrounding pH (ideally within about one pH unit), not far removed from it — a distant pKa leaves the buffer mostly in one form and poorly able to donate or accept protons.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rapid loss of the buffer from the system would reduce, not increase, its concentration and therefore its buffering capacity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buffering is most effective when the base and acid forms are present in comparable amounts (ratio near 1:1); a markedly unequal ratio leaves little capacity to absorb a change in the direction that is already predominant.

questions.title: Which of the following increases the glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf)?
questions.question: Which of the following increases the glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf)?

options.A: An increase in the surface area of the glomerular capillary membrane
options.C: Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, as in diabetic nephropathy
options.D: A reduction in the number of functioning nephrons

explanations.A: Correct. The filtration coefficient (Kf) is the product of the glomerular capillary's hydraulic permeability and its total available surface area for filtration, so any increase in that surface area — for example, mesangial cell relaxation that opens more capillary loops to filtration — raises Kf. Kf sets how much fluid crosses the glomerular capillary wall for a given net filtration pressure, so a larger effective filtering surface directly increases the filtrate produced at the same driving pressure. Conditions that reduce capillary surface area or damage the filtration membrane lower Kf and, all else equal, lower GFR.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Afferent arteriolar constriction lowers glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and reduces GFR through the pressure term of the Starling equation, not through Kf.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Basement membrane thickening, as in diabetic nephropathy, reduces the hydraulic permeability of the filtration barrier and so decreases Kf.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fewer functioning nephrons means less total glomerular capillary surface area available for filtration, which decreases the whole-kidney Kf.

questions.title: What is the major functional role of the juxtamedullary nephrons?
questions.question: What is the major functional role of the juxtamedullary nephrons?

options.C: Filtering the bulk (majority) of renal plasma flow
options.D: Serving as the exclusive site of renin secretion

explanations.A: Correct. Juxtamedullary nephrons have unusually long loops of Henle that plunge deep into the medulla, and their glomeruli are served by vasa recta that follow the same hairpin course. This anatomical arrangement is what builds and preserves the corticomedullary osmotic gradient through countercurrent multiplication and exchange, which is the mechanism the kidney uses to produce urine that is either concentrated or dilute depending on ADH status. Cortical nephrons, which have short loops confined largely to the cortex, contribute much less to this concentrating mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Whole-kidney autoregulation of GFR is a property of renal blood vessels generally (myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms), not a role specific to juxtamedullary nephrons.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The great majority (roughly 85%) of nephrons are cortical nephrons, and they receive the bulk of renal plasma flow and filtration; juxtamedullary nephrons are the minority.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renin is secreted by juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole, which are present at nephrons throughout the cortex, not exclusively at juxtamedullary nephrons.

questions.title: The renal transport maximum (Tm) for a substance is best defined as which of the following?
questions.question: The renal transport maximum (Tm) for a substance is best defined as which of the following?

options.A: The maximal rate at which the renal tubules can reabsorb or secrete that substance
options.B: The plasma concentration at which the substance first appears in the urine
options.C: The glomerular filtration rate at which filtration exactly equals excretion of the substance
options.D: The rate of glomerular filtration once plasma protein binding of the substance is saturated

explanations.A: Correct. Tm describes a carrier-mediated transport ceiling: once the tubular transporters responsible for reabsorbing or secreting a substance (such as glucose, phosphate, or PAH) become fully saturated, the rate of transport cannot increase further no matter how much more filtered load or delivered substrate is presented. This maximal, saturable rate is what Tm measures, and it is a property of the transport system's capacity rather than of glomerular filtration itself. Tm-limited transport contrasts with gradient-time-limited transport, which has no fixed maximal rate and instead depends on tubular flow and contact time.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That description is the renal threshold, a related but distinct concept — the plasma concentration at which the filtered load first begins to exceed Tm so the substance starts to spill into the urine, not the Tm itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tm is defined at the level of tubular transport capacity, not by a filtration rate at which excretion equals filtration.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasma protein binding affects how much of a substance is freely filterable, but it is not what defines the tubular transport maximum.

questions.learning_objective: The renal transport maximum (Tm) is the maximal rate at which the tubules can reabsorb or secrete a substance

questions.title: Which of the following best characterizes the vasa recta?
questions.question: Which of the following best characterizes the vasa recta?

options.C: The primary site of renin secretion in the kidney
options.D: A capillary network that is impermeable to water and solutes

explanations.A: Correct. The vasa recta are the peritubular capillaries that follow the hairpin course of the juxtamedullary loops of Henle, and they operate purely as a passive countercurrent exchanger: blood equilibrates by diffusion with the surrounding hyperosmotic interstitium as it descends and again as it ascends, without any active pumping of solute by the vessel wall itself. Because their descending and ascending limbs run in parallel and exchange solute and water passively along the way, the vasa recta remove the reabsorbed water and solute from the medulla without washing out the osmotic gradient that the loop of Henle actively builds. This passive design is precisely what distinguishes the vasa recta from the loop of Henle, which multiplies the gradient by active transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Active countercurrent multiplication of the medullary gradient is performed by the loop of Henle, particularly the actively transporting thick ascending limb, not by the vasa recta.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renin is secreted by juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole, an entirely different vascular structure from the vasa recta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vasa recta are, in fact, highly permeable to both water and solutes — that permeability is what allows them to equilibrate passively with the medullary interstitium.

questions.learning_objective: The vasa recta function as a passive countercurrent exchange system

questions.title: A serum potassium concentration of 2.5 mEq/L (hypokalemia) can occur secondary to which of the following acid-base disturbances?
questions.question: A serum potassium concentration of 2.5 mEq/L (hypokalemia) can occur secondary to which of the following acid-base disturbances?

explanations.A: Correct. In alkalosis, cells buffer the fall in extracellular hydrogen ion by releasing H+ from inside the cell in exchange for extracellular K+ moving in, driving a transcellular shift of potassium into cells. Alkalosis also increases distal tubular potassium secretion, both because more bicarbonate is delivered to the distal nephron and because the cells there favor K+ secretion when intracellular H+ is low, so alkalosis characteristically produces or worsens hypokalemia. This combination of an intracellular shift and enhanced renal loss is why hypokalemia and alkalosis so often occur together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute metabolic acidosis typically shifts potassium out of cells (as cells buffer excess H+ partly by exchanging it for intracellular K+), producing hyperkalemia rather than hypokalemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Respiratory acidosis similarly tends to shift potassium out of cells and is associated with hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic renal failure impairs renal potassium excretion and is classically associated with hyperkalemia, the opposite of the potassium level described.

questions.title: Which of the following is a renal compensatory mechanism in respiratory acidosis?
questions.question: Which of the following is a renal compensatory mechanism in respiratory acidosis?

options.A: Increased renal tubular hydrogen ion secretion
options.D: Decreased sodium-hydrogen exchange in the proximal tubule

explanations.A: Correct. When a chronically raised arterial PCO2 lowers blood pH in respiratory acidosis, the kidney compensates over one to several days by increasing tubular hydrogen ion secretion (largely via the proximal and distal Na+/H+ exchangers and H+-ATPases), which both regenerates and increases net reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate and increases new bicarbonate generation through enhanced ammoniagenesis and titratable acid excretion. The net effect is a rise in plasma bicarbonate that partially restores pH toward normal despite the persistently elevated PCO2. This renal compensation is slower than the immediate intracellular buffering that occurs in acute respiratory acidosis, which is why the compensatory bicarbonate rise is most prominent in the chronic form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased bicarbonate excretion is the renal response to alkalosis, not acidosis — in respiratory acidosis the kidney instead reclaims and generates more bicarbonate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal compensation for acidosis increases, not decreases, ammoniagenesis, since ammonia production and excretion as ammonium is a major route for generating new bicarbonate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Proximal Na+/H+ exchange activity increases, not decreases, during renal compensation for acidosis, driving greater hydrogen ion secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption.

questions.learning_objective: The kidney compensates for respiratory acidosis by increasing tubular hydrogen ion secretion and new bicarbonate generation

questions.title: Chronic liver disease with hypoalbuminemia characteristically leads to which of the following?
questions.question: Chronic liver disease with hypoalbuminemia characteristically leads to which of the following?

options.A: A decrease in plasma (colloid) osmotic pressure
options.B: An increase in plasma oncotic pressure
options.D: An increase in glomerular filtration rate

explanations.A: Correct. Impaired hepatic synthetic function in chronic liver disease reduces plasma albumin production, and because albumin is the principal contributor to plasma colloid (oncotic) osmotic pressure, hypoalbuminemia lowers plasma oncotic pressure. This fall in the force that normally opposes fluid movement out of capillaries favors fluid escape into the interstitium and body cavities, contributing to the edema and ascites characteristic of advanced liver disease. The same fall in effective circulating volume also activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and non-osmotic ADH release, which is why cirrhotic patients often retain sodium and water despite a low measured plasma osmolality.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypoalbuminemia lowers, rather than raises, plasma oncotic pressure, since albumin is its main determinant.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The reduced effective arterial blood volume of advanced liver disease non-osmotically stimulates, rather than suppresses, ADH secretion, contributing to dilutional hyponatremia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Advanced liver disease is typically associated with reduced effective renal perfusion and a falling, not rising, glomerular filtration rate, particularly in hepatorenal physiology.

questions.title: Which specific mechanism is responsible for preserving (rather than dissipating) the hyperosmolarity of the renal medullary interstitial fluid once it has been established?
questions.question: Which specific mechanism is responsible for preserving (rather than dissipating) the hyperosmolarity of the renal medullary interstitial fluid once it has been established?

options.A: The passive countercurrent exchange mechanism of the vasa recta
options.B: Active sodium chloride transport by the thick ascending limb
options.C: Facilitated urea transport across the inner medullary collecting duct
options.D: ADH-mediated insertion of aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct

explanations.A: Correct. The medullary osmotic gradient is actively built by the loop of Henle (chiefly active NaCl reabsorption by the thick ascending limb) and reinforced by urea recycling, but that gradient would be washed away by ordinary blood flow if it were not for the vasa recta's hairpin, passive countercurrent exchange arrangement, which lets blood equilibrate with the interstitium on the way in and the way out so that it carries away reabsorbed water and solute without net dissipation of the gradient. This preserving role is distinct from the active processes that generate the gradient in the first place. Because the vasa recta run parallel to the loop of Henle and exchange passively rather than pump solute, they act as countercurrent exchangers rather than multipliers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Active thick ascending limb transport is what generates (multiplies) the medullary gradient in the first place, rather than what preserves it against washout by blood flow, which is specifically the vasa recta's role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Urea recycling contributes to establishing part of the inner medullary gradient, but it is not the mechanism that prevents the gradient from being washed out by medullary blood flow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aquaporin-2 insertion determines how much water the collecting duct reabsorbs in response to ADH; it does not preserve the medullary interstitial gradient against dissipation by blood flow.

questions.learning_objective: The passive countercurrent exchange mechanism of the vasa recta preserves medullary interstitial hyperosmolarity against washout

questions.title: Which of the following statements regarding the renal handling of inulin is true?
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the renal handling of inulin is true?

options.A: It is freely filtered at the glomerulus but is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the renal tubules
options.B: It is freely filtered and then partially reabsorbed by the proximal tubule
options.C: It is actively secreted into the tubular fluid in addition to being filtered
options.D: It is extensively bound to plasma proteins and therefore poorly filtered

explanations.A: Correct. Inulin is a small, biologically inert polysaccharide that is freely filtered across the glomerular capillary (it is not protein bound) and, once filtered, is neither reabsorbed nor secreted anywhere along the nephron. Because the amount excreted in the urine per unit time therefore exactly equals the amount filtered per unit time, inulin clearance is numerically equal to GFR, which is precisely why it is used as the classic gold-standard exogenous marker for measuring glomerular filtration rate. Any substance that were reabsorbed or secreted would give a clearance that under- or overestimates true GFR, which inulin avoids.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inulin is not reabsorbed at all by the tubules; any reabsorption would make its clearance lower than true GFR, defeating its purpose as a GFR marker.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inulin is not secreted; a secreted marker (such as PAH) yields a clearance that overestimates GFR and instead approximates renal plasma flow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inulin is not protein bound and is freely filterable at the glomerulus, which is a requirement for it to serve as an accurate GFR marker.

questions.learning_objective: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, making its clearance equal to GFR

questions.title: Which of the following conditions characteristically causes hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis?
questions.question: Which of the following conditions characteristically causes hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis?

explanations.A: Correct. Diarrheal fluid is rich in bicarbonate, so severe diarrhea causes a large gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate; the body retains chloride to maintain electroneutrality as bicarbonate falls, producing a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. Because no unmeasured anion accumulates in this process — bicarbonate is simply lost and replaced by chloride — the anion gap stays normal, distinguishing it from the high-anion-gap acidoses. This is one of the classic causes of normal anion gap ('hyperchloremic') metabolic acidosis taught alongside renal tubular acidosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diabetic ketoacidosis accumulates unmeasured ketoacid anions (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate), producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis rather than a hyperchloremic one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lactic acidosis accumulates lactate, an unmeasured anion, and so also produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Salicylate poisoning classically produces a mixed picture with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (from accumulated organic acids) alongside a respiratory alkalosis, not a simple hyperchloremic acidosis.

questions.title: Which of the following is a recognized endocrine function of the kidney?
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized endocrine function of the kidney?

explanations.A: Correct. The kidney's juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin, an enzyme that cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and so initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; this is one of the kidney's several recognized endocrine roles, alongside its secretion of erythropoietin and its activation of vitamin D to calcitriol. Renin release is triggered by falling afferent arteriolar pressure, reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa, and increased renal sympathetic activity, making it a key hormonal link between renal perfusion and systemic blood pressure and volume regulation. This distinguishes renin, an enzyme-hormone produced by the kidney itself, from hormones that merely act on the kidney.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone is secreted by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, not by the kidney; the kidney is a target organ for aldosterone, not its source.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ADH (vasopressin) is synthesized by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary; the kidney is its target organ, not its source.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cortisol is secreted by the adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata), not by the kidney.

questions.title: What is the underlying cause of renal glucosuria, a benign condition distinct from diabetic glucosuria?
questions.question: What is the underlying cause of renal glucosuria, a benign condition distinct from diabetic glucosuria?

options.A: A decreased renal threshold for glucose reabsorption
options.B: An increased filtered load of glucose from hyperglycemia
options.C: Destruction of the glomerular filtration barrier

explanations.A: Correct. Renal (or 'renal') glucosuria results from an isolated, usually inherited defect in the proximal tubular glucose transporters (chiefly SGLT2), which lowers the tubular transport maximum and hence the plasma glucose concentration ('threshold') at which glucose begins to appear in the urine. Because plasma glucose itself is normal or only mildly elevated, this differs fundamentally from diabetic glucosuria, where the tubular transport machinery is normal but the filtered load of glucose exceeds a normal Tm because plasma glucose is very high. Isolated renal glucosuria is typically a benign, asymptomatic finding with no associated hyperglycemia or diabetes-related complications.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An increased filtered load from hyperglycemia is the mechanism of diabetic glucosuria, in which the transport machinery itself is normal but is simply overwhelmed by a high filtered glucose load — the opposite mechanism from renal glucosuria.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal glucosuria does not involve damage to the glomerular filtration barrier; glomerular filtration of glucose is normal, and the defect is purely tubular.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renal glucosuria is not caused by increased renal blood flow; the defect lies in tubular glucose transport capacity, not in filtration or perfusion.

questions.title: What effect does afferent arteriolar dilation have on renal blood flow (RBF)?
questions.question: What effect does afferent arteriolar dilation have on renal blood flow (RBF)?

options.C: It has no effect on RBF
options.D: It decreases RBF while increasing the filtration fraction

explanations.A: Correct. Dilating the afferent arteriole lowers the resistance of the vessel that lies upstream of the glomerulus, which increases blood flow into the glomerular capillaries and raises both renal blood flow and glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. Because both resistance vessels (afferent and efferent arterioles) determine total renal vascular resistance, reducing afferent resistance specifically increases flow into the kidney rather than restricting it. This is the opposite of the effect produced by afferent arteriolar constriction, which reduces both RBF and GFR together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dilation lowers vascular resistance, which increases, not decreases, blood flow through the dilated vessel.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because the afferent arteriole is a major resistance vessel controlling flow into the glomerulus, its diameter has a substantial effect on RBF, not no effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Afferent dilation increases, rather than decreases, RBF, and because both RBF and GFR tend to rise together with afferent dilation, filtration fraction (GFR/RPF) is not simply increased in the way efferent constriction would produce.

questions.title: Which of the following is a recognized adverse effect of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) administration?
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized adverse effect of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) administration?

options.D: Hypocalcemia-induced tetany from alkalosis alone, without any effect on potassium

explanations.A: Correct. Administering sodium bicarbonate raises extracellular pH, and the resulting alkalemia drives potassium into cells in exchange for hydrogen ions moving out to help buffer the change, producing a transcellular shift that lowers plasma potassium. Alkalinization also increases distal tubular potassium secretion by favoring the electrochemical gradient for K+ exit into the tubular lumen, compounding the fall in plasma potassium. This is why bicarbonate therapy is used cautiously, and why potassium is monitored, in patients being treated with it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. NaHCO3-induced alkalosis characteristically causes hypokalemia through the mechanisms above, rather than hyperkalemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate is alkalinizing and, if anything, corrects rather than worsens metabolic acidosis; that is its intended pharmacologic effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alkalosis from bicarbonate administration can lower ionized calcium and occasionally contribute to tetany, but this occurs alongside, not instead of, the well-recognized potassium shift, so this option's claim that potassium is unaffected is incorrect.

questions.title: The combination of metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia together is most characteristic of which of the following?
questions.question: The combination of metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia together is most characteristic of which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. As chronic kidney disease advances, the kidneys progressively lose the capacity both to excrete the daily hydrogen ion load (through reduced ammoniagenesis and reduced acid excretion) and to excrete potassium (through a reduced number of functioning nephrons and reduced distal tubular flow and aldosterone responsiveness), so metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia commonly coexist in chronic renal failure. This combination is a hallmark of advanced kidney disease and is part of why potassium and acid-base status are closely monitored as kidney function declines. Together they also promote cardiac arrhythmia risk, which is one reason severe hyperkalemia in renal failure is treated urgently.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prolonged vomiting causes loss of hydrogen ion and chloride from gastric secretions, producing metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia, not acidosis with hyperkalemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes increased renal potassium and hydrogen ion secretion, producing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, the opposite pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Severe diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate-rich, potassium-containing fluid, producing metabolic acidosis together with hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.

questions.title: Which of the following increases renin secretion from the juxtaglomerular cells?
questions.question: Which of the following increases renin secretion from the juxtaglomerular cells?

options.C: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa

explanations.A: Correct. Juxtaglomerular cells are richly innervated by sympathetic nerve fibers, and increased renal sympathetic activity stimulates renin release through beta-1 adrenergic receptors on these cells, independent of the pressure and macula densa pathways. This sympathetic pathway is one of the three classic stimuli for renin secretion (alongside the intrarenal baroreceptor mechanism and the macula densa mechanism) and is particularly important during states such as hemorrhage or standing, when sympathetic tone rises before other signals change. Because it acts through a distinct receptor mechanism, sympathetic stimulation can increase renin release even when renal perfusion pressure is unchanged.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased afferent arteriolar perfusion pressure is sensed by the intrarenal baroreceptor mechanism as a signal of adequate renal perfusion and suppresses, rather than increases, renin release.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa signals an adequate or excessive GFR and, through the macula densa feedback mechanism, decreases renin secretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atrial natriuretic peptide directly suppresses renin release from the juxtaglomerular apparatus as part of its overall natriuretic, volume-lowering actions.

questions.title: An increase in peritubular capillary oncotic pressure, and the resulting rise in proximal tubular fluid reabsorption that follows it, is the physiological basis of which of the following regulatory phenomena?
questions.question: An increase in peritubular capillary oncotic pressure, and the resulting rise in proximal tubular fluid reabsorption that follows it, is the physiological basis of which of the following regulatory phenomena?

explanations.A: Correct. When GFR rises, a larger fraction of renal plasma flow is filtered (a higher filtration fraction), which concentrates plasma proteins in the blood that continues on into the peritubular capillaries and so raises peritubular capillary oncotic pressure; this higher oncotic pressure pulls proportionally more of the reabsorbed proximal tubular fluid back into the capillaries. The net result is that proximal tubular fractional reabsorption rises in step with GFR, keeping the fraction of filtered load reabsorbed roughly constant despite changes in GFR — this coupling is precisely what is called glomerulotubular balance. It is a passive, physical (Starling-force) phenomenon operating at the level of the peritubular capillary and proximal tubule, distinct from the feedback signaling mechanisms that regulate GFR itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tubuloglomerular feedback is a distinct mechanism in which the macula densa senses distal NaCl delivery and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone to regulate GFR, not a mechanism driven by peritubular capillary oncotic pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pressure natriuresis describes how a rise in renal perfusion pressure directly increases sodium excretion, a different, longer-term blood pressure regulatory mechanism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osmotic diuresis is caused by an unreabsorbed solute (such as glucose in uncontrolled diabetes) holding water in the tubular lumen, an unrelated mechanism to peritubular capillary Starling forces.

questions.title: Regarding the renal handling of water along the nephron, which of the following is correct?
questions.question: Regarding the renal handling of water along the nephron, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Only a small fraction of the filtered water (on the order of a few percent) is reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct, chiefly under the influence of ADH
options.B: The majority of filtered water (around two-thirds) is reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct
options.C: No filtered water is ever reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct, regardless of ADH status
options.D: All remaining tubular water is reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct irrespective of ADH levels

explanations.A: Correct. Of the water filtered at the glomerulus, roughly two-thirds is reabsorbed obligatorily in the proximal convoluted tubule, with further amounts reabsorbed in the descending thin limb and, when ADH is present, in the distal tubule and cortical collecting duct; only a small remaining percentage of the original filtered water reaches the medullary collecting duct, where ADH-driven aquaporin-2 insertion allows a further, variable, but quantitatively small fraction to be reabsorbed to produce concentrated urine. This final, ADH-dependent step in the medullary collecting duct is what allows fine control of urine concentration and body water balance, even though it involves only a modest fraction of the total filtered water. Without ADH, this segment remains relatively water-impermeable and that last increment of water is instead excreted as dilute urine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reabsorption of about two-thirds of filtered water occurs in the proximal convoluted tubule, not in the medullary collecting duct, which handles only a small final fraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. In the presence of ADH, the medullary collecting duct does reabsorb a small but physiologically important fraction of filtered water via aquaporin-2 channels; this segment is not always impermeable to water.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct is ADH-dependent, not fixed; without ADH this segment remains relatively water-impermeable and that remaining water is excreted rather than reabsorbed.

questions.title: A patient presents with the nephritic syndrome — hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, and mild proteinuria. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.question: A patient presents with the nephritic syndrome — hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, and mild proteinuria. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. Post-infectious glomerulonephritis, classically following a streptococcal throat or skin infection, is an immune-complex-mediated proliferative glomerulonephritis that produces the nephritic syndrome: hematuria (often with red cell casts), hypertension and oliguria from reduced GFR and sodium retention, and only mild ('nephritic-range') proteinuria, in contrast to the heavy proteinuria of nephrotic disease. This constellation reflects glomerular inflammation with capillary wall disruption (allowing red cells through) and reduced filtration, rather than the massive protein leak of an intact but hyperpermeable filtration barrier. Most cases in children are self-limited, with recovery over weeks.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Minimal change disease is a cause of the nephrotic, not the nephritic, syndrome — it presents with heavy proteinuria and edema but typically normal blood pressure and no hematuria.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy is also a nephrotic-syndrome disease, presenting with heavy proteinuria from subepithelial immune deposits rather than with the hematuria and hypertension of a nephritic picture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renal amyloidosis characteristically causes a nephrotic-range proteinuria, not the hematuria-and-hypertension-predominant nephritic syndrome.

questions.title: An 11-year-old child has non-selective, mild proteinuria that fails to respond to a full course of corticosteroid therapy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.question: An 11-year-old child has non-selective, mild proteinuria that fails to respond to a full course of corticosteroid therapy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. In children, steroid-resistant nephrotic-range proteinuria is the classic clinical clue pointing away from minimal change disease and toward focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), a lesion in which segmental scarring of some glomeruli is associated with less selective proteinuria (loss of larger proteins in addition to albumin) and a poorer response to corticosteroids. FSGS is now recognized as a leading cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in the pediatric population and often requires alternative immunosuppressive strategies or is associated with an underlying podocyte-injury process. Its histology (segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis affecting only a subset of glomeruli) distinguishes it from the diffusely normal-appearing glomeruli of minimal change disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome and is characteristically steroid-responsive, with proteinuria typically resolving on corticosteroid therapy — the opposite of the scenario described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy is uncommon in children and classically presents in adults; it is not the typical explanation for a steroid-resistant nephrotic child.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis produces a nephritic, not a proteinuria-predominant nephrotic, picture, and is self-limited rather than treated with courses of corticosteroids for proteinuria.

questions.title: A sexually active young woman presents with fever, an elevated urinary white cell count with white cell casts, and costovertebral angle (loin) pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.question: A sexually active young woman presents with fever, an elevated urinary white cell count with white cell casts, and costovertebral angle (loin) pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. The combination of fever, pyuria with white cell casts, and costovertebral angle tenderness indicates infection that has ascended beyond the bladder to involve the renal parenchyma and collecting system — acute pyelonephritis. White cell casts specifically localize the infection to the kidney (they can only form within the renal tubules), distinguishing pyelonephritis from a purely lower urinary tract infection, and the systemic fever together with flank pain reflects parenchymal and perinephric inflammation. Sexual activity is a well-recognized risk factor for ascending urinary tract infection (including the classic 'honeymoon cystitis' pattern) that can progress to pyelonephritis if untreated.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Uncomplicated cystitis is confined to the bladder and typically causes dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort without fever, white cell casts, or costovertebral angle tenderness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute interstitial nephritis is usually a drug-hypersensitivity reaction associated with eosinophiluria and a recent new-drug exposure, not an ascending infection with white cell casts and flank pain.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis characteristically produces red cell casts and hematuria from glomerular capillary injury, not white cell casts, which specifically indicate tubulointerstitial/infectious inflammation.

questions.title: A 24-year-old man presents with bilateral renal cysts. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in a gene encoding a ciliary membrane protein. Which of the following gene products is most likely affected?
questions.question: A 24-year-old man presents with bilateral renal cysts. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in a gene encoding a ciliary membrane protein. Which of the following gene products is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Correct. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, which typically presents in young adulthood with bilateral renal cysts, is caused by mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, which encode polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 — ciliary membrane proteins expressed on the primary cilium of tubular epithelial cells that normally help sense luminal flow and regulate epithelial cell proliferation and tubular architecture. Loss of normal polycystin function ('ciliopathy') disrupts this signaling and leads to progressive cyst formation and enlargement in both kidneys over decades. This adult-onset, autosomal dominant presentation is the classic teaching pairing distinguishing it from the infantile, autosomal recessive form of polycystic kidney disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrocystin (encoded by PKHD1) is the gene product implicated in autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, which classically presents in infancy or childhood rather than at age 24.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aquaporin-2 is the ADH-regulated water channel of the collecting duct; mutations in it cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not cystic kidney disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) mutations cause autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease, a distinct, non-cystic hereditary nephropathy.

questions.title: A child sustains a crush injury complicated by acute kidney injury, from which there is complete recovery. Which of the following is the most likely underlying renal lesion?
questions.question: A child sustains a crush injury complicated by acute kidney injury, from which there is complete recovery. Which of the following is the most likely underlying renal lesion?

explanations.A: Correct. Crush injury causes acute kidney injury chiefly through rhabdomyolysis: myoglobin released from damaged muscle is directly toxic to and obstructs the renal tubules (compounded by hypovolemia and renal vasoconstriction), producing acute tubular necrosis. Because the basement membrane underlying the injured tubular epithelial cells typically remains intact in ATN, the epithelium is capable of regenerating from surviving basal cells, which is why ATN — unlike lesions that destroy the underlying architecture — is classically reversible with supportive care, matching the complete recovery described. This reversibility is a key distinguishing clinical feature of ATN among the causes of acute kidney injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with crescent formation, tends to cause a fulminant and often irreversible decline in renal function rather than complete recovery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal cortical necrosis is an ischemic lesion that destroys the renal cortex including the tubular basement membranes, and is typically irreversible, unlike the reversible course described.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis develops over a long period with progressive, largely irreversible scarring, not as an acute, fully reversible event after a single crush injury.

questions.title: A 36-year-old woman with advanced cervical carcinoma is found on CT scan to have pelvic spread. If this is not surgically or medically corrected, which of the following renal complications is she most likely to develop?
questions.question: A 36-year-old woman with advanced cervical carcinoma is found on CT scan to have pelvic spread. If this is not surgically or medically corrected, which of the following renal complications is she most likely to develop?

explanations.A: Correct. Advanced cervical carcinoma classically spreads locally into the parametrium, where it can directly invade or compress the distal ureters as they pass close to the cervix; untreated ureteric obstruction from this pelvic spread leads to progressive back-pressure changes in the collecting system — hydronephrosis — and, if bilateral or affecting a solitary functioning kidney, can progress to obstructive renal failure. This mechanical, obstructive complication is one of the recognized life-threatening consequences of untreated locally advanced cervical cancer, and ureteric obstruction with hydronephrosis is part of the staging assessment for the disease. It is a direct anatomical consequence of tumor bulk on the ureter rather than a metastatic or immune-mediated process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cervical carcinoma spreading to the pelvis does not cause a separate primary renal cell carcinoma to develop; the two are unrelated malignancies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute glomerulonephritis is an immune-mediated glomerular process, not a recognized complication of local tumor spread from cervical cancer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renal artery stenosis is typically due to atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia affecting the renal artery itself, not a consequence of pelvic tumor spread compressing the ureters.

questions.title: Which of the following is a characteristic light and electron microscopic finding in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)?
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic light and electron microscopic finding in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)?

options.A: "Tram-track" splitting of the glomerular basement membrane with subendothelial immune deposits
options.B: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes with no identifiable immune deposits
options.C: Subepithelial "spike-and-dome" deposits along the glomerular basement membrane
options.D: Linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane

explanations.A: Correct. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is characterized by mesangial cell proliferation and mesangial interposition into the glomerular capillary wall, together with subendothelial immune complex deposits; on silver or PAS staining, the interposed mesangium and reduplicated basement membrane produce the classic 'tram-track' (double-contour) appearance. This combination of proliferative and membrane-splitting changes, driven by subendothelial deposits, is what distinguishes MPGN from purely proliferative or purely membranous glomerular diseases and often produces a mixed nephritic-nephrotic clinical picture. Type I MPGN in particular shows this tram-track pattern with subendothelial deposits most classically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diffuse podocyte foot process effacement without deposits is the defining electron microscopic finding of minimal change disease, not MPGN.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits are the classic finding in membranous nephropathy, a different disease from MPGN.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Linear IgG deposition along the GBM is the hallmark of anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, not MPGN, which instead shows granular immune-complex deposits.

questions.title: A defect in the enzyme 21-alpha-hydroxylase is most likely to result in which of the following electrolyte abnormalities?
questions.question: A defect in the enzyme 21-alpha-hydroxylase is most likely to result in which of the following electrolyte abnormalities?

explanations.A: Correct. 21-alpha-hydroxylase is required for adrenal synthesis of both cortisol and aldosterone; in its classic, severe (salt-wasting) form, 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes markedly reduced aldosterone production, which impairs renal sodium retention and potassium excretion, producing hyponatremia together with hyperkalemia and a salt-wasting crisis in affected infants. The enzyme block also shunts steroid precursors toward androgen synthesis, which is why congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency also causes virilization, but the electrolyte disturbance itself follows directly from the mineralocorticoid deficiency. This salt-wasting presentation is a medical emergency in neonates if unrecognized.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone deficiency from 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes renal sodium loss and hyponatremia, not sodium retention and hypernatremia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 21-hydroxylase deficiency is not characteristically associated with hypocalcemia; its electrolyte hallmark is the sodium/potassium disturbance from mineralocorticoid deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The acid-base disturbance in salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency is metabolic acidosis (from hyperkalemia and volume depletion), not alkalosis.

questions.title: Mesangial cell proliferation with mesangial IgA deposition is the characteristic finding in which of the following conditions?
questions.question: Mesangial cell proliferation with mesangial IgA deposition is the characteristic finding in which of the following conditions?

explanations.A: Correct. IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is defined immunohistologically by mesangial proliferation together with dominant mesangial deposition of IgA (often with C3 and IgG), reflecting abnormal handling of poorly galactosylated IgA1 immune complexes that lodge in the mesangium and trigger a proliferative response. It is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and classically presents with episodic macroscopic hematuria, often coinciding with mucosal (upper respiratory or gastrointestinal) infections, distinguishing it from the delayed, post-infectious timing of post-streptococcal GN. The mesangial IgA-dominant deposit pattern on immunofluorescence is the key diagnostic feature separating it from other glomerulonephritides.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis shows subepithelial 'humps' with dominant IgG and C3 deposition on immunofluorescence, following streptococcal infection by one to several weeks, not mesangial IgA deposition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane, not mesangial IgA deposits, and presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Minimal change disease shows no significant immune deposits by immunofluorescence or electron microscopy; its defining lesion is podocyte foot process effacement.
