questions.title: Which of the following is a characteristic clinical and histologic feature of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease?
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic clinical and histologic feature of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease?

options.A: Segmental necrosis with crescent formation from parietal epithelial cell proliferation
options.B: Diffuse podocyte foot process effacement without crescents
options.C: Subepithelial "spike-and-dome" deposits along the basement membrane

explanations.A: Correct. Anti-GBM disease is caused by circulating autoantibodies directed against an epitope on the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular (and, in Goodpasture syndrome, alveolar) basement membrane; the resulting complement-mediated injury produces segmental fibrinoid necrosis of the glomerular tuft with proliferation of parietal (Bowman's capsule) epithelial cells into the urinary space, forming crescents. This crescentic, necrotizing pattern produces a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis clinically, with a characteristic linear (rather than granular) pattern of IgG deposition along the GBM on immunofluorescence. Because the antibody attacks a structural basement membrane antigen directly, the resulting injury is typically severe and rapidly destructive if untreated.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Isolated podocyte foot process effacement without crescents describes minimal change disease, a very different, non-inflammatory podocytopathy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits are characteristic of membranous nephropathy, not anti-GBM disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dominant mesangial IgA deposition is the hallmark of IgA nephropathy; anti-GBM disease instead shows linear GBM staining, not mesangial IgA deposits.

questions.title: A patient with chronic bronchiectasis develops the nephrotic syndrome. Which of the following is the most likely underlying renal pathology?
questions.question: A patient with chronic bronchiectasis develops the nephrotic syndrome. Which of the following is the most likely underlying renal pathology?

explanations.A: Correct. Chronic suppurative or inflammatory conditions such as bronchiectasis sustain persistently elevated levels of the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A protein, fragments of which can be deposited extracellularly in tissues (including the glomeruli) as AA amyloid; renal AA amyloidosis characteristically produces heavy, nephrotic-range proteinuria and progressive kidney disease. This secondary (reactive) amyloidosis is a recognized long-term complication of any chronic inflammatory or infective disease process, and bronchiectasis with recurrent or chronic pulmonary suppuration is a classic predisposing condition taught alongside rheumatoid arthritis and chronic osteomyelitis. Renal biopsy in this setting classically shows Congo red-positive, apple-green birefringent deposits under polarized light.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Minimal change disease is not associated with chronic suppurative lung disease; it is typically idiopathic (or occasionally linked to lymphoma or NSAID use), unrelated to bronchiectasis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diabetic nephropathy requires a background of diabetes mellitus, which is not part of this clinical picture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy can rarely be secondary to chronic infection, but the classic teaching pairing for chronic suppurative disease such as bronchiectasis is secondary (AA) amyloidosis, not membranous nephropathy.

questions.title: A ureteric stone is impacted at the level of the transpyloric plane. Which of the following anatomical narrowings of the ureter does this correspond to?
questions.question: A ureteric stone is impacted at the level of the transpyloric plane. Which of the following anatomical narrowings of the ureter does this correspond to?

options.B: The pelvic brim, where the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels
options.D: The mid-ureteric point at the level of the ischial spine

explanations.A: Correct. The transpyloric plane (of Addison), a horizontal plane roughly at the level of the L1 vertebra, passes through the hila of the kidneys and the renal pelvis, close to where the renal pelvis narrows into the ureter — the pelviureteric junction (PUJ). Because it is the first, and narrowest, of the three classic sites of physiological ureteric narrowing, the PUJ is a common site for a stone descending from the renal pelvis to become impacted, and its level corresponds closely to the transpyloric plane. This anatomical correlation is a standard teaching point linking surface/vertebral landmarks to the sites of ureteric stone impaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pelvic brim, where the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels, is the second classic narrowing and lies well below the transpyloric plane, at the level of the sacroiliac joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vesicoureteric junction, where the ureter enters the bladder, is the most distal ureteric narrowing and lies in the pelvis, far below the transpyloric plane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ischial spine level is closer to the vesicoureteric/pelvic segment of the ureter, not to the transpyloric plane, which corresponds to the renal pelvis/PUJ level.

questions.title: Uric acid (urate) renal stones, as seen in gout, are typically characterized by which of the following?
questions.question: Uric acid (urate) renal stones, as seen in gout, are typically characterized by which of the following?

options.A: Smooth, yellow-brown stones that are radiolucent and may occasionally form large staghorn-shaped calculi
options.B: Rough, black, spiculated stones that are strongly radio-opaque
options.C: Stones that form characteristically in alkaline urine
options.D: Stones composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite)

explanations.A: Correct. Uric acid stones, which form in patients with gout or other hyperuricosuric states, are classically smooth and yellow-brown and, because they lack calcium, are radiolucent on plain X-ray (visible on CT or ultrasound instead); while pure struvite (infection) stones are the most typical cause of large staghorn calculi, sufficiently persistent uric acid stone formation can occasionally also fill and cast the renal pelvis and calyces in a staghorn-like configuration. Uric acid stones form characteristically in persistently acidic urine, which favors precipitation of the poorly soluble undissociated uric acid form. Management therefore includes urinary alkalinization in addition to reducing uric acid production or excretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rough, black, radio-opaque stones describe calcium oxalate stones, not uric acid stones, which are smooth, yellow-brown and radiolucent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Uric acid stones form in acidic, not alkaline, urine; alkaline urine instead favors struvite and calcium phosphate stone formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones are a distinct stone type associated with urease-producing bacterial infection, not with gout or uric acid metabolism.

questions.learning_objective: Gout-associated uric acid stones are smooth, yellow-brown and radiolucent, and can occasionally form staghorn calculi

questions.title: Which of the following types of renal stone characteristically appears brownish-black in color?
questions.question: Which of the following types of renal stone characteristically appears brownish-black in color?

explanations.A: Correct. Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of renal stone and are classically rough, spiculated, and brownish-black in color, a pigmentation attributed to the incorporation of blood breakdown products (hemosiderin) from the mucosal trauma these irregular stones cause as they form and pass. They are also strongly radio-opaque on plain X-ray because of their calcium content, in contrast to the radiolucent uric acid stones. Their rough surface is what predisposes to hematuria and pain even before the stone has fully obstructed the urinary tract.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Uric acid stones are smooth and yellow-brown, not the rough, brownish-black stones described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Struvite stones are typically dirty white to grey and associated with urease-producing infection, not classically brownish-black.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cystine stones have a characteristic yellowish, waxy appearance, distinct from the brownish-black color of calcium oxalate stones.

questions.title: Renal blood flow (RBF) remains relatively constant (autoregulated) across which range of mean arterial pressure (MAP)?
questions.question: Renal blood flow (RBF) remains relatively constant (autoregulated) across which range of mean arterial pressure (MAP)?

options.D: Only a single fixed pressure value, not a range

explanations.A: Correct. Renal blood flow and GFR are autoregulated to remain relatively constant across a mean arterial pressure range of approximately 80 to 180 mmHg, mainly through myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms acting on the afferent arteriole. Within this range, a rise in perfusion pressure triggers afferent arteriolar constriction (and a fall triggers dilation), keeping glomerular capillary pressure and flow nearly steady despite the swings in systemic pressure. This protects the kidney's filtration function from ordinary fluctuations in blood pressure during daily activity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A range of 40 to 80 mmHg lies mostly below the lower limit of renal autoregulation; below approximately 80 mmHg, autoregulatory mechanisms are exhausted and renal blood flow begins to fall in parallel with pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A range of 180 to 220 mmHg lies mostly above the upper limit of autoregulation; sustained pressures this high exceed the myogenic mechanism's compensatory capacity and can instead damage the renal vasculature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Autoregulation operates across a range of pressures, not at one fixed value; that is precisely what allows the kidney to maintain stable flow despite everyday variation in systemic blood pressure.

questions.title: Which of the following is completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) under normal physiological conditions?
questions.question: Which of the following is completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) under normal physiological conditions?

options.A: Glucose, amino acids, and filtered protein

explanations.A: Correct. Under normal filtered loads, the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids via specific sodium-coupled cotransporters, and it also reclaims virtually all of the small amount of protein that is filtered, through receptor-mediated endocytosis. This near-complete reabsorption is why glucose and amino acids are normally absent from the final urine despite being freely filtered at the glomerulus. It also explains why even modest glomerular or tubular protein leak is clinically significant, since the PCT's endocytic capacity for protein is a finite, saturable process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Urea is only partially reabsorbed passively along the nephron (roughly half of the filtered load in the proximal tubule, with more complex handling in the medullary collecting duct); it is not completely reabsorbed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatinine is freely filtered and not meaningfully reabsorbed; a small amount is even secreted, which is why creatinine clearance is used clinically to estimate GFR.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inulin is the classic marker that is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted at all, which is exactly why its clearance is used as the gold-standard measure of GFR.

questions.learning_objective: The proximal convoluted tubule normally reabsorbs essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids, and virtually all filtered protein via receptor-mediated endocytosis

questions.title: An extracellular fluid (ECF) osmolarity of approximately 300 mOsm/L indicates which of the following?
questions.question: An extracellular fluid (ECF) osmolarity of approximately 300 mOsm/L indicates which of the following?

options.A: Osmotic equilibrium between the extracellular and intracellular fluid compartments
options.B: Severe extracellular fluid hypertonicity relative to the intracellular compartment
options.C: Ongoing net water movement from the intracellular to the extracellular compartment
options.D: A laboratory error, since normal plasma osmolarity is far lower than 300 mOsm/L

explanations.A: Correct. Because cell membranes are freely permeable to water, water moves rapidly across them until osmotic equilibrium is reached; at steady state the osmolarity of the extracellular fluid and intracellular fluid are equal, both approximately 275 to 295 (commonly rounded to ~300) mOsm/L. An ECF osmolarity in this normal range therefore reflects an intracellular fluid that is in osmotic equilibrium with it, not a state of active fluid shift. This is the baseline against which clinical disturbances such as hyponatremia, hypernatremia, and dehydration are recognized as deviations.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An ECF osmolarity of about 300 mOsm/L is within the normal physiological range, not a hypertonic state; hypertonicity would be reflected by osmolarity values well above this normal range with a corresponding transcellular water shift.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Net water movement between compartments occurs only when there is an osmotic gradient between them; at 300 mOsm/L with the two compartments in equilibrium, there is no net driving force for water shift in either direction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Approximately 275 to 295, often rounded to 300, mOsm/L is the accepted normal range for plasma/ECF osmolarity, not an erroneous value.

questions.learning_objective: An extracellular fluid osmolarity of approximately 300 mOsm/L reflects osmotic equilibrium between the extracellular and intracellular fluid compartments

questions.title: Which functional role is most characteristic of cortical nephrons, as distinct from juxtamedullary nephrons?
questions.question: Which functional role is most characteristic of cortical nephrons, as distinct from juxtamedullary nephrons?

options.A: They are chiefly responsible for renal autoregulation of blood flow and GFR
options.B: They are chiefly responsible for generating the medullary osmotic gradient that concentrates urine
options.C: They possess the longest loops of Henle in the kidney
options.D: They are the only nephrons that contain a glomerulus

explanations.A: Correct. Cortical nephrons, which have short loops of Henle that barely dip into the outer medulla, make up about 85 percent of nephrons and are the ones chiefly credited with renal autoregulation of blood flow and GFR via their well-developed juxtaglomerular apparatus and myogenic/tubuloglomerular feedback responses. Their glomeruli and juxtaglomerular apparatus sit near the corticomedullary junction, where autoregulatory feedback signaling is most active. This functional division of labor contrasts with juxtamedullary nephrons, whose long loops instead specialize in generating the medullary concentration gradient.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Generating the medullary osmotic gradient that concentrates urine is the specialized role of juxtamedullary nephrons, with their long loops of Henle and closely associated vasa recta, not of cortical nephrons.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Juxtamedullary nephrons, not cortical nephrons, have the longest loops of Henle, penetrating deep into the medulla; cortical nephron loops are short.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Every nephron, cortical or juxtamedullary, contains a glomerulus; the distinction between the two nephron types is based on the location of the glomerulus and the length of the loop of Henle, not the presence of a glomerulus.

questions.learning_objective: Cortical nephrons, with their short loops of Henle, are chiefly responsible for renal autoregulation of blood flow and GFR

questions.title: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the renal medullary circulation?
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the renal medullary circulation?

options.A: Sluggish (slow) blood flow through the vasa recta
options.B: The vasa recta receive the majority (about 90 percent) of total renal blood flow
options.C: Vasa recta blood flow is driven by active pumping of the medullary capillary walls
options.D: Vasa recta flow rate has no bearing on the medullary concentration gradient

explanations.A: Correct. The vasa recta, the specialized peritubular capillaries that dip alongside the loops of Henle into the medulla, carry a deliberately sluggish, low blood flow, only a small fraction of total renal blood flow. This slow flow, combined with their hairpin countercurrent arrangement, is exactly what allows them to act as passive countercurrent exchangers, taking up water and solute without washing out the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. Faster flow would progressively dissipate the gradient that the loop of Henle works to establish.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vasa recta receive only a small fraction, not the majority, of total renal blood flow; the bulk of renal blood flow perfuses the cortex, which needs high flow to support glomerular filtration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vasa recta exchange is entirely passive, driven by diffusion and osmotic/hydrostatic gradients between the descending and ascending limbs, not active pumping by the capillary wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vasa recta's sluggish flow is directly responsible for preserving the medullary concentration gradient; faster flow would wash out the gradient and impair the kidney's ability to concentrate urine.

questions.learning_objective: The vasa recta carry a sluggish, low blood flow, which helps preserve the medullary interstitial osmotic gradient

questions.title: In which of the following patient groups is treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria specifically indicated?
questions.question: In which of the following patient groups is treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria specifically indicated?

options.C: Elderly patients with long-term indwelling catheters who are otherwise asymptomatic
options.D: Diabetic patients with well-controlled blood glucose and no urinary symptoms

explanations.A: Correct. Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is reserved for specific high-risk groups in whom untreated bacteriuria carries a meaningful risk of progressing to serious infection, including pregnant women, patients undergoing an invasive urologic procedure, and neutropenic or otherwise significantly immunosuppressed patients, who lack the normal inflammatory response needed to contain a urinary infection. In neutropenic patients, an unaddressed bacteriuria can progress rapidly to bacteremia and sepsis because of the impaired neutrophil-mediated defense. Screening and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in this group is therefore standard practice, unlike in the general population.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in healthy, non-pregnant premenopausal women is not treated; screening and treatment in this group provides no benefit and only promotes antibiotic resistance and side effects.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is expected and near-universal in long-term catheterized patients; guidelines specifically recommend against screening or treating it in this group unless the patient becomes symptomatic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Diabetes alone, without pregnancy, immunosuppression, or an upcoming urologic procedure, is not by itself an indication to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in current guidelines.

questions.title: Which of the following pigments is characteristically produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in culture?
questions.question: Which of the following pigments is characteristically produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in culture?

options.B: Prodigiosin (a red pigment produced by Serratia marcescens)
options.C: Violacein (a purple pigment produced by Chromobacterium violaceum)

explanations.A: Correct. Pseudomonas aeruginosa characteristically produces pyocyanin, a blue-green, water-soluble pigment (along with the yellow-green fluorescent pigment pyoverdine), which diffuses into the surrounding culture medium and gives infected wounds, sputum, or urine a distinctive blue-green color. This pigment production, together with a grape-like or corn-tortilla-like odor and oxidase positivity, is a classic bedside and laboratory clue to Pseudomonas infection. Pyocyanin also has redox activity that contributes to the organism's virulence by generating reactive oxygen species in host tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prodigiosin is the characteristic red pigment of Serratia marcescens, an unrelated gram-negative organism, not Pseudomonas.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Violacein is a purple pigment produced by Chromobacterium violaceum, a distinct and much rarer gram-negative organism, not Pseudomonas.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Brown pigmentation from bilirubin breakdown is not a recognized culture characteristic of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.title: "Honeymoon cystitis" (acute cystitis related to recent sexual intercourse) caused by a gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, penicillin-resistant bacillus is most likely due to which organism?
questions.question: "Honeymoon cystitis" (acute cystitis related to recent sexual intercourse) caused by a gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, penicillin-resistant bacillus is most likely due to which organism?

explanations.A: Correct. "Honeymoon cystitis" refers to acute uncomplicated cystitis precipitated by sexual intercourse, which can introduce periurethral bacteria into the bladder; Escherichia coli, a gram-negative, lactose-fermenting bacillus that is intrinsically resistant to penicillin via beta-lactamase and outer-membrane permeability barriers, is by far the leading cause of this presentation, as it is for uncomplicated UTI generally. Its fimbriae allow it to adhere to uroepithelium, and its lactose-fermenting, gram-negative morphology on culture is a standard identifying feature distinguishing it from other uropathogens. This combination of clinical context and organism characteristics is a classic exam pairing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a gram-positive coccus, not a gram-negative, lactose-fermenting bacillus, even though it is also a recognized cause of cystitis in young sexually active women.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enterococcus faecalis is a gram-positive coccus, not a gram-negative bacillus, so it does not match the described organism morphology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus, not a bacillus, and does not ferment lactose; it causes urethritis/cervicitis rather than this classic cystitis picture.

questions.title: Which of the following correctly characterizes Proteus vulgaris, in contrast to Proteus mirabilis?
questions.question: Which of the following correctly characterizes Proteus vulgaris, in contrast to Proteus mirabilis?

options.A: It is indole-positive and tends to be more antibiotic-resistant
options.B: It is indole-negative and uniformly antibiotic-susceptible
options.C: It is a gram-positive organism, unlike Proteus mirabilis
options.D: It does not cause urinary tract infection or produce urease

explanations.A: Correct. Proteus vulgaris is indole-positive, which distinguishes it biochemically from the far more common Proteus mirabilis (indole-negative), and it also tends to be more broadly antibiotic-resistant than P. mirabilis. Like other Proteus species it is strongly urease-positive, predisposing to struvite (infection) stone formation and alkaline urine, and displays swarming motility on culture. Correctly separating P. vulgaris from P. mirabilis by the indole test is a classic microbiology identification point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Indole-negative is the characteristic of Proteus mirabilis, not Proteus vulgaris, which is indole-positive; and P. vulgaris is not uniformly antibiotic-susceptible.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proteus vulgaris is a gram-negative bacillus, like all Proteus species, not gram-positive.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Proteus vulgaris is a recognized, urease-producing cause of urinary tract infection, notably associated with struvite stone formation, not an organism unrelated to the urinary tract.
